newsitem.title: USA: AOL cuts prices, and consumers get more choices.
newsitem.headline: AOL cuts prices, and consumers get more choices.

text.p: - It finally happened.

After months of foot dragging, America Online has unveiled a lower, flat-fee price for unlimited use of the online network, matching prices with major competitors and reflecting the general tumult in the Internet access business.

Beginning Dec. 1, AOL subscribers can pay $19.95 a month for unlimited time online -- $14.95 a month if they sign up for two years in advance -- or for occasional users, $4.95 for three hours plus $2.50 an hour.

For the first time, the company separated programming from access, allowing consumers to pay $9.95 a month to use AOL chat rooms and view other AOL-only content while logging on through an existing Internet connection.
Internet analysts gave the moves mixed reviews, saying lower fees could hurt profit margins initially but ultimately help AOL collect new customers and solidify its brand name.
But what does it mean for consumers?
For AOL subscribers, it's great, said Peter Krasilovsky, analyst with Arlen Communications in Bethesda, Md.

"They've leveled the playing field and provide superior content services," Krasilovsky said. "Nothing matches them if your goal is going online to use (their) content, but if your goal is to surf, you might find them slower than a pure Internet provider."
For people who're considering going online for the first time, it means price isn't the issue it once was, although some differences remain.
AT&T WorldNet, for example, charges $19.95 a month for unlimited time online, but offers five free hours a month for a year to long-distance customers who sign up for the service.

Microsoft Network also charges $19.95 a month for unlimited access, but when a revamped version of the network debuts in early November, subscribers who log on through an existing Internet connection will pay only $6.95 a month for MSN content, or $69.95 if they sign up for a year in advance.

CompuServe offers two flat-fee prices -- $17.95 a month for its family-friendly WOW network, and $19.95 a month for its Sprynet Internet access service -- but hasn't instituted unlimited-use prices for its flagship online network, although the company is looking into it, a spokeswoman said.

Price isn't the only factor to consider when deciding on an Internet access provider. That's especially true for beginners who aren't as familiar with the online landscape and need more hand holding, experts said. Other essentials to consider include:

-- Phone lines, or what the industry calls "points of presence" or POPs. The more POPs an Internet access provider offers, the more likely a consumer can dial in for free using a local phone number, and the less likely they'll be hung up by busy signals. In the United States, America Online has 500 POPs, Microsoft has 320, and AT&T WorldNet has 215, and will add 40 more by year-end, said Tom Evslin, AT&T WorldNet vice president.

-- Access speed, or the rate at which consumers receive information. Most online networks and national Internet access providers offer 28.8 bits per second modem connections on most or all POPs. Microsoft Network supports faster connections in parts of its network, and many major access providers are testing 56.6 bps modem connections or plan to begin tests soon.

-- Software, or the programmes an individual uses to go online and accomplish tasks such as reading mail, posting messages to discussion groups, browsing the World Wide Web and downloading software. America Online has been heralded for its intuitive, easy-to-use software interface, and superior chat and e-mail. Version 3.0, introduced for Windows 3.1 users in July and announced Tuesday for Windows 95 and Mac, replaces the company's proprietary Web browser with Microsoft's Internet Explorer Web browser and includes other improvements.

Competitors CompuServe, Prodigy and Microsoft Network have also upgraded to Internet Explorer -- subscribers can also use Netscape Navigator if they choose. More importantly, all three have redesigned their entire services to live on the Web, so content resembles Web pages and subscribers can easily jump between the service's proprietary areas and the Web.

-- Customer support. Most online services and Internet access providers run online help desks and provide toll-free telephone support, although not all companies offer assistance 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

-- Programming, or original content that is unique to a service. America Online has been a leader, partnering with more than 1,000 so-called content providers ranging from major publishers to cyberspace entrepreneurs. When it relaunches next month, MSN will open six "channels" with 20 original programmes as well as areas for investing, travel, and MSNBC, the company's news joint venture with NBC.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
